prize_parts.citation: For the discovery of exact fluctuation relations and the development of stochastic thermodynamics, extending the second law to small systems driven far from equilibrium

statement.case_for: Fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics changed what the second law means for small systems. The Evans-Searles and Jarzynski relations are exact statements about fluctuating work and entropy production far from equilibrium, and Seifert's trajectory-level definitions of work, heat and entropy turned them into a general framework. The ideas are original and conceptually simple. They have been tested independently in RNA and DNA pulling experiments, colloids and single-electron devices, and they are now the standard language for molecular motors and nanoscale engines. A prize here would honour a result about a basic law and not a method or a device. Having listened to colleagues, I still think this is the strongest case in terms of conceptual novelty per unit of attribution ambiguity, once the credit is limited to three people. The experimental record is stable after more than two decades.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is attribution. Four names are credited, any three-person choice omits a decisive contributor (Crooks, whose detailed fluctuation theorem is close to Jarzynski's, or Searles and Cohen/Morriss on the early theorem), and it is a theory-dominated candidate with no single dramatic observation to point to. Only I ranked it first, so it has narrow opening support on this committee, and I must allow that my closeness to the stochastic-process community inflates its attractiveness to me. Its relevance to the broad field of physics may also be judged smaller than a new quantum state of matter or a new instrument.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp quantum spin Hall work first as a clean prediction followed by a decisive experimental discovery of a nameable phenomenon, while acknowledging that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree that B044 is a real discovery and that its confirmation is broad. But the attribution problem he names is not minor. The HgTe proposal that made Molenkamp's experiment possible, and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele and Moore-Balents, sit outside the credited set, so any Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves a visible gap in the chain from prediction to observation. That is a comparable difficulty to my own Crooks problem, not a decisive advantage for B044. The 2016 prize on topological phases also reduces its novelty in the eyes of the Academy, which I think Danielsson understates. I rank it as my first alternative because the support for it is real.

responses.point: Kroll puts the optical lattice clock first as the clearest case of better measurement opening new physics, with a clean two-person credit (Katori and Ye) and consequences for the redefinition of the second, geodesy and constant tests.
responses.response: This is the most compact attribution on the shortlist and I take the point seriously. My reservation is that lattice clocks are a refinement of a measurement programme the Academy has already rewarded in 2005 and 2012, and the new physics is still prospective, mostly in constraints and proposed searches. I would not call the concern fatal, and I accept Kroll's argument that a precision instrument can be an invention in its own right. I place B024 as my second alternative and would support it if the committee wants a metrology prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first for lasting impact on strongly correlated electrons and on quantitative materials modelling, while noting that Metzner and Müller-Hartmann are not credited and that DMFT is a framework rather than a single discovery.
responses.response: I ranked B037 fourth for the same reasons he does: the impact is deep and the impurity mapping is elegant. But I am less convinced that it fits a prize built around a discovery, because the omission of Metzner is built into the trio and the physics result is a controlled approximation scheme. The fluctuation-theorem case is a statement that holds exactly, and I would put that distinction in the committee's discussion. I do not treat DMFT as a weaker candidate in scientific terms.

responses.point: Lindroth supports optical lattice clocks first and places Bloch-Greiner-Zoller and the topological insulator work next, flagging that choosing three from five cold-atom names is hard and that the 2016 topological prize may reduce appetite for further topological recognition.
responses.response: I agree with her caution on both the five-name cold-atom candidate and the topological overlap, and her point strengthens my view that cleanly bounded credit is a real virtue. Where I differ is that she treats clean credit as sufficient; it should be weighed together with how fundamental the result is, and there I think the fluctuation relations score higher than a clock.

uncertainties: Whether a three-person allocation of Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert can be defended against the Crooks and Searles claims, and whether the committee would rather split the framing between fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics.
Whether the committee will see statistical-physics theory with a more limited experimental face as competitive with the discovery-led candidates that dominate the opening ballots.
I have not independently checked the full experimental confirmation record or the priority details, and I rely on my recollection of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented work on stochastic processes is close in subject to the field of B016, but I have no documented collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to any credited name, and I would flag the proximity of subject only as context.
